summary.text: 走 is interpreted in early forms as a running person, and a clear verbal use meaning “run” is reported in Western Zhou bronze writing. In modern Chinese it commonly means “walk” or “go on foot.”

formation.text: The oldest proposed construction is pictographic: an early graph is interpreted as a person running with swinging arms. Some later bronze forms are analyzed as adding 止 to emphasize the feet. The received Shuowen account instead reads the seal-script form as 夭 plus 止, explaining 夭 as bending; this records a Han-era analysis and differs from the account of the earliest graph.

history.text: The graph is recorded in oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms, with later forms increasingly altered. A modern digital rendering of the Shuowen seal-script tradition illustrates the received 夭-and-止 analysis; it does not establish the earliest structure.

In the standardized graph, the upper shape is 土 and the lower shape is 龰. These visible parts do not show that 土 was an original semantic component; the early upper figure is interpreted as a running person, later read as 夭 in the Shuowen tradition.

uncertainties.text: Analyses differ over whether the earliest graph depicts a running person and whether later bronze forms added 止. The Shuowen decomposition belongs to a separate historical analysis.

Oracle-bone examples are reported in place-name and personal-name contexts and do not establish an earlier verbal use. A clear verb meaning “run” is reported in a Western Zhou bronze inscription, but the evidence does not supply a securely dated first occurrence.
The documented senses of fleeing, going toward, and walking do not establish a complete chronology or a certain path of semantic development.

senses.text: A clear verbal use is reported in the bronze-inscription phrase 夙夜奔走. The cited oracle-bone examples are reported as names or place names, not secure verbal attestations.
Classical citations use 走 for fleeing or escaping. Their witnesses are not securely dated here, and they do not show when this sense developed in relation to “run.”
A historical sense “go or tend toward” is recorded, but the cited material does not establish its chronology relative to “run” or “flee.”
In modern use, 走 commonly means walking or going on foot. The evidence does not establish when this broader sense became current or how it developed from the older “run” sense.

limitations.text: The evidence supports a Western Zhou bronze use meaning “run,” but not a securely dated first use. The cited oracle-bone examples are not independently established as verbs.
The sources document fleeing, going toward, and walking, but do not establish their chronology or semantic connections.

evidence.text: Someone 土 stepping with their foot 止
Pictograph of a person swaying their arms while walking.
趨也。从夭、止。夭止者，屈也。凡走之屬皆从走。

Pictogram (象形): a running man. An additional 止 (“foot”) was added later. The variant form 𧺆 preserves the form in the Small Seal Script.
In the modern form, the top component (夭) is simplified to the unrelated 土 and the bottom part is stylized as 龰. See also the top component of 去 and 赤.
As with 圭, there are two separate vertical strokes, not a single one.
Schuessler (2007) considers this to be part of a large Sino-Tibetan word family, including 搜 (OC *sru, “to move”), 速 (OC *sloːɡ, “quick”), 夙 (OC *suɡ, “morning”), 聳 (OC *sloŋʔ, “to excite”), 蔌 (OC *sloːɡ, “vegetables”), which derive from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *m-sow (“to arise; to awake”).
趨也。从夭、止。夭止者，屈也。凡走之屬皆从走。

evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle-bone and early bronze forms as a person running with arms swinging; later bronze forms add 止 to emphasize the feet. This is a modern paleographic account, distinct from Xu Shen’s historical analysis.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The entry transcribes oracle-bone examples 合集17230 as “貞：王往走災” and 合集27939 as “貞：其令(命)亞走馬.” It classifies the first as a place name and the latter as a personal-name use; therefore these attestations do not independently establish the verbal sense “run.” The entry reports “run” as a basic sense and cites clearer verbal contexts in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions. The specific object of 走馬 here is a horse, but the graph is not thereby a horse pictogram.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.text: Lists oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, Shuowen seal, clerical, and regular-script records, including oracle-bone Heji 27939, early Western Zhou 大盂鼎 (集成2837), and Western Zhou to Warring States bronze forms. Its account says the oracle-bone graph depicts a person running with swinging arms; later bronze graphs may add elements including 止, after which it interprets the earlier figure as a phonetic as well as semantic element. It describes Warring States and seal forms as continuing bronze forms, then clerical and regular forms as increasingly altered. This later phonetic-component interpretation is an analysis of later structures, not evidence that the oldest graph was a phonetic compound.

evidence.text: The dictionary gives the classical verb sense “run” with citations including 《詩·大雅·緜》“來朝走馬,” 《儀禮·士相見禮》“某將走見,” 《孟子·梁惠王上》“棄甲曳兵而走,” and 《韓非子·五蠹》“兔走觸株.” It separately gives fleeing, moving toward, and later walking uses. These are lexicographic citations to texts of varying composition/transmission histories; the page does not date each manuscript witness, so they should not be presented as securely dated first occurrences.

evidence.text: The dictionary separates run, flee, go/tend toward, walk, travel, visit, leak, lose, servant, and other senses, with later textual examples for several. The broad modern sense “walk/go on foot” differs from the classical run sense; the page supplies examples but not a complete dated pathway establishing when each semantic extension arose. Treat the paths from running to fleeing, going toward, and ordinary walking as plausible semantic developments that need sense-specific chronological evidence, not as chronology inferred from the order of a gloss list.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.
